passage:
I'm Swati. Neelam and I share a room in a working women's hostel in Indore, and for a month I've watched her play a real-money card game on her phone every night.
At first it was small. Then she had a bad week, maybe nine or ten losses in a row; I heard her counting. Instead of stopping, she started topping up more each time. "After this many losses, a win is coming. It has to," she told me once, not looking up.
Last Sunday she asked to borrow money for the mess bill. She has never asked before.
I don't know exactly what's going on in her head. She might be scared. She might think she's nearly there. Tonight I'm going to sit on her bed and ask, gently, how much she has actually lost, and whether we can talk to the warden together.

qa.q: What did Neelam ask to borrow money for last Sunday?
qa.a: She asked to borrow money for the mess bill.

qa.q: Going by what she tells Swati, why does 'a win is coming' make sense to Neelam?
qa.a: Neelam feels hopeful that after nine or ten losses a win is owed, so topping up looks like getting closer to it rather than digging deeper.

qa.q: Is Swati's plan for tonight a good turning point, and why?
qa.a: Yes; asking gently how much Neelam has lost and offering to go to the warden together brings the problem into the open without shaming her.

qa.q: What is it like for Swati to watch this every night?
qa.a: Swati seems worried and unsure, noticing the changes without knowing what Neelam feels, which makes the borrowing request stand out even more.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman top up more after each loss, sure a win is due.

Week 1, Monday: Ojas, twenty-one, bought two lottery tickets at the counter near the station, same as every morning. Nothing again. "Twenty-three days without even a small prize," he told Trisha. "It has to hit soon."
Week 3, Thursday: He was buying ten a day now, with part of his stipend. "The longer it goes, the closer I am," he said. Trisha frowned. "Each draw starts from zero, Ojas. It doesn't know about the other days."
Week 5, Saturday: Ojas skipped their movie night, saying he was short of cash. When Trisha borrowed a pen from his bag, a thick bundle of losing tickets slid out. She sat down next to him. "Can we talk about this? I'm not angry. I'm worried."

qa.a: He was buying ten a day.

qa.q: Why does 'the longer it goes, the closer I am' feel true to Ojas?
qa.a: Ojas feels hopeful that each loss is a step toward a win that is owed, so buying more seems like making sure he is there when it finally comes.

qa.a: It lets Ojas talk without feeling judged, which is more likely to help him stop than a lecture.

qa.q: What are the five weeks like from Trisha's side?
qa.a: Trisha watches a friend drift from a small habit to skipping plans, and the bundle of tickets turns her unease into real worry.

passage:
Madhav, sit a minute. I saw your phone at lunch, those cricket odds. Let me tell you about myself at twenty.
I was a skinny boy in a college hostel then. One of the boys took me to the racecourse. I lost the first race. And the second. By the fifth I was sure: I had lost so many, the next one had to be mine. So I doubled. Lost. Doubled again. I wasn't thinking about horses any more; I was only thinking, "It's due."
By evening I had spent my whole month's hostel money. I walked six kilometres back because I didn't have bus fare. I told my father on the phone that night, my voice shaking. He didn't shout. He said, "Losing streaks don't owe you anything, Darshan. Come home this weekend."
I'm not lecturing you. I'm only telling you where "it's due" took me.

qa.q: How did Darshan get back after spending his hostel money?
qa.a: He walked six kilometres back because he didn't have bus fare.

qa.q: What does 'I wasn't thinking about horses any more' reveal about Darshan at twenty?
qa.a: It reveals he had stopped judging each race and was driven only by a desperate, stubborn feeling that a win was owed after so many losses.

qa.q: What choice in Darshan's story stopped the losses from growing further?
qa.a: Telling his father that night, even with a shaking voice, brought in someone who calmly helped him step away.

qa.q: How might Madhav hear this story, given the cricket odds on the phone?
qa.a: Madhav may feel caught out at first, but hearing a story rather than a lecture could make it easier to look honestly at the betting.

grounding: A senior tells Madhav how believing a win was due made him double his racecourse bets until he lost a month's money.

passage:
The power went out at eleven, and Lavanya's phone was at nine percent. Rent was due to the landlady at eight the next morning, and the envelope in her drawer was already eight hundred short from what she had lost that evening on a card-flip game on a betting site.
"Eight losses in a row," she whispered to Sarika in the dark. "Nobody loses nine. The next one has to be mine."
She bet four hundred. Lost. Six percent.
"It's even more due now," Lavanya said, and took the next eight hundred from the envelope.
Sarika sat up and held out a hand. "Give me the phone till the lights come back. Please."
The screen dimmed at two percent. Lavanya stared at it, the envelope much thinner now, before she finally let go.

qa.q: When was the rent due to the landlady?
qa.a: At eight the next morning.

qa.q: How does Lavanya feel as the losses pile up, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lavanya feels desperate and falsely hopeful, whispering that the next one has to be hers and taking more money from the rent envelope after each loss.

qa.q: At which point could Lavanya have stopped the losses from growing, and what could help her now?
qa.a: Before taking money from the envelope; handing the phone to Sarika then would have saved the rent. Now, being honest with someone she trusts and talking to a counsellor about the betting could help.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika lying in the dark while Lavanya keeps betting?
qa.a: Sarika is probably frightened for Lavanya and for the rent, feeling helpless until deciding to ask for the phone.

grounding: It shows a young adult who keeps betting because a win feels due after a losing streak, while the losses grow under a deadline.

passage:
Between deliveries, Pranav parked his scooter outside a Pune bakery and opened the colour-prediction game again. Red, green or violet, a new round every minute. He had lost six rounds since lunch, so he pressed green for two hundred. Six reds, he told himself. Green has to come.
Red.
By evening he had lost four thousand, more than a week of his delivery pay. Each time he raised the bet, because surely a streak that long was nearly over.
At home, his sister Vidya saw the bank messages glowing on his phone while it charged. "Pranav, what is this?"
"It'll balance out. One green and I'm back."
"You said that about the reds, didn't you?" she asked quietly.
He opened his mouth to explain and found he had nothing new to say.

qa.q: How much had Pranav lost by evening?
qa.a: Four thousand, more than a week of his delivery pay.

qa.q: How does Pranav feel after each loss, and what does he do?
qa.a: Pranav feels hopeful that a green is overdue and desperate to win back his losses, so he raises the bet each time.

qa.q: What turning point does Vidya's question create, and what could Pranav choose next?
qa.a: Vidya's question leaves Pranav with nothing new to say; he could choose then to stop playing, remove the game and ask for help from someone he trusts or a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel seeing the bank messages?
qa.a: Vidya is likely shocked and worried; her quiet voice suggests she wants to understand rather than shout at her brother.

passage:
Dear Ganga,
I need to tell someone who won't judge me. You know the card app I started playing in April, just for fun? I've lost about thirty thousand rupees. It started small. Then I had a bad week, and I kept thinking, after this many losses a win is due; the app can't keep beating me. So I played more, and bigger, to catch the win when it came. It never came the way I thought.
Last night I sat on the hostel stairs until 3 a.m. and realised the cards don't know I've been losing. Each hand is new.
This morning I told Didi everything. She's coming on Saturday, and we have an appointment with the college counsellor on Monday. I've deleted the app.
Can you call me tonight? I don't want to be alone with this.
Nandini

qa.q: How much has Nandini lost?
qa.a: About thirty thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep playing bigger after losing?
qa.a: Nandini felt sure a win was due after so many losses and was desperate to catch it, so bigger bets felt like the way back.

qa.q: What steps has Nandini taken, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Telling Didi, booking the college counsellor, deleting the app and asking Ganga to call, so the problem is shared with people who can help.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Ganga would probably feel worried but glad Nandini reached out, and want to call that night.

grounding: A student writes that believing a win was due after a losing streak led to bigger bets and growing losses, and describes seeking help.

passage: Minakshi, thanks for having me. I'm Sarita, and two years ago I was betting on cricket matches through an app on my phone. At first it was small. Then I lost five bets in a row, and something in my head said, "The next one's yours. It's due." So I bet bigger. And lost. And bet bigger again. Every loss made me more sure the win was coming, as if the universe kept a scoreboard. It doesn't. Each match is just a match. By the time I understood, I'd lost my semester fees. What stopped me was my roommate finding me crying over my phone at 2 a.m. She didn't lecture me. She sat with me and called a gambling helpline on speaker, right then. Now I help run a support group on campus. The win was never due. Help was.

qa.q: When did the roommate find Sarita crying?
qa.a: At 2 a.m.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep betting bigger?
qa.a: Sarita felt sure a win was due after the losing run, as if the universe kept a scoreboard, so each loss made the next bet feel safer.

qa.q: What did the roommate do, and why was it the right response?
qa.a: She stayed calm, sat with Sarita and called a gambling helpline on speaker straight away, getting real help that night instead of a lecture.

qa.q: What might the roommate have felt finding Sarita at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and worried, yet steady enough to stay and call for help.

Week one. Ira downloaded a colour-prediction game a hostel friend swore by: guess red or green, win double. She lost the first four rounds, then won one. "See, it balances," she told Naveen. He shrugged.
Week three. Ira had lost her mess money for the month. Red had come up seven times in a row the night before, so she put everything on green. Red again. "It's due," she kept whispering. "It has to switch." She skipped dinner to keep playing.
Week five. Naveen found her in the library, not studying, just staring at the screen, eyes red. "How much?" She told him. He didn't say "I told you." He walked with her that evening to the student welfare office, where the counsellor stayed late to talk with her and helped her block the app. Walking back, Ira said quietly, "Red didn't owe me anything."

qa.a: Her mess money for the month.

qa.q: Why did Ira put everything on green?
qa.a: She felt sure, almost desperate, that after seven reds a switch to green was due, as if the game remembered.

qa.a: Naveen was probably worried and sad to see her eyes red, but calm enough to take her for help.

passage: Devika, you're asking why I never play cards for money at weddings. Let your Ganga Maasi tell you. When I was twenty, at my cousin's wedding in Nagpur, the young people played teen patti late into the night. I lost the first three rounds. Then five. Everyone said, "Your turn will come, Ganga." I believed it. After so many losses, a win had to be close. So I bet more each time, to get it all back at once. By two in the morning I had lost the gold bangles my mother had given me for the wedding. I sat on the terrace and cried. My mother found me. She didn't shout. She went that same night to the cousin who had won them, and she brought them back, and she made me promise. The cards never owed me anything.

qa.q: What did young Ganga lose by two in the morning?
qa.a: The gold bangles her mother had given her for the wedding.

qa.q: Why did young Ganga keep betting more after each loss?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and desperate, believing that after so many losses a win had to be close.

qa.q: Which choice in the story stopped the losses from growing?
qa.a: Her mother coming that same night, calmly getting the bangles back and making Ganga promise, which ended the chasing.

qa.q: How might Ganga's mother have felt finding her on the terrace?
qa.a: She was probably upset and worried, but chose calm help over shouting.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a young adult, betting more at cards because a win felt due after a losing streak, and losing her bangles.

passage: Maria had come to the casino boat in Panaji with her flatmate Dolma for one hour, just to see it. Three hours later she was still at the roulette table, and the last ferry back left at midnight. She had bet on black ten times. Red had come up nine. "Black's due," she muttered. "It's been red forever." She doubled her bet. Red. She had now lost her rent money for the month. Dolma grabbed her arm. "Maria, we're going to miss the ferry." "One more. It has to come." Dolma stood between her and the table. "It doesn't have to. The wheel doesn't remember." On the ferry, Maria sat shaking, staring at the black water. At home, Dolma found the number for a gambling helpline and sat beside her while she called.

qa.q: How many times had red come up out of Maria's ten bets on black?
qa.a: Red had come up nine.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she said "It has to come"?
qa.a: She felt desperate and stubborn, sure black was due after so much red, and couldn't stop.

qa.q: What did Dolma do, and why was it a good response?
qa.a: She physically stopped Maria, explained the wheel doesn't remember, got her to the ferry, and sat with her while she called a gambling helpline that night.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt standing between Maria and the table?
qa.a: Dolma was probably frightened and determined, worried about her friend and the last ferry.

grounding: Shows a young adult under time pressure betting bigger at roulette because a win feels due after a losing streak, until a friend steps in.

passage: In their Mumbai flat, Tejas had been betting on cricket matches through an app for a month. He'd lost five bets in a row. "My luck's due to turn," he told Eshaan, his flatmate, at breakfast. "Six losses in a row almost never happens." He put more on the evening match than on the last three together. Eshaan watched him refresh the score all day, not eating. The team lost. Tejas sat on the balcony, pale. "Tomorrow for sure. I'll get it all back." Eshaan sat down beside him. "Tejas, each match doesn't care about the last. You're chasing." "I know how cricket works." "It's not cricket. It's the betting." Tejas didn't answer. That night Eshaan called Tejas's elder brother, and the next morning the brother came, and the three of them looked up a counselling service together.

passage:
Last December, on a college trip to Goa, I walked onto a casino boat with Pooja just to see. I'm Simran, and I'm writing this so I remember it properly.
At the roulette table, black came up seven times in a row. Seven. I was sure red was coming, like the wheel was holding its breath. I put five hundred on red. Black. I doubled. Black again. By the time Pooja pulled my arm, I had lost most of the money I'd saved for the whole trip.
The worst part was the feeling in my chest. Not fear. Excitement. Every loss made red feel more certain.
Pooja paid for my dinner and didn't say "I told you so" once. Back at college I told my mother everything, and we talked properly about money for the first time. I haven't been near a table since.

qa.q: How many times in a row did black come up?
qa.a: Black came up seven times in a row.

qa.q: What did Simran feel as the losses grew?
qa.a: Simran felt excited rather than afraid, and each loss made red feel more certain, which kept the betting going.

qa.q: What could Simran do if a streak ever feels due again?
qa.a: Simran could walk away, as happened when Pooja pulled Simran's arm, and talk to a trusted person before chasing any loss.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt watching at the table?
qa.a: Pooja was likely worried and uneasy, pulling Simran's arm, and afterwards chose kindness over 'I told you so'.

grounding: Shows a young adult who kept betting because a win seemed due after a streak, and whose losses grew.

passage:
Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block 2. Written by Pema, resident warden.
Lalremsiami, second year, came to my office tonight at nine to ask for an advance on her mess refund. When I asked why, she showed me her phone: an online card game, eleven losses in a row this week.
She said, "It has to turn now. I've lost too many times for it to keep going." She sounded very sure, and very tired. She said each loss made her bet more, to win it all back at once.
I didn't argue about luck. I told her the losses were not a sign that a win was coming, and that asking for help was a good step, not a shameful one.
What I did next: I called the college counsellor on duty while she sat with me and booked her in for 10 a.m. I also gave her a gambling helpline number, and she chose to delete the game in front of me.

qa.q: How many losses in a row had Lalremsiami had this week?
qa.a: Lalremsiami had eleven losses in a row this week.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami keep raising her bets?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt sure the game had to turn, and each loss made her more desperate to win it all back at once.

qa.q: Why was calling the counsellor while Lalremsiami sat there a good step?
qa.a: It turned a late request into real help that same evening, with a 10 a.m. session and a helpline number, instead of a lecture about luck.

qa.q: How did the evening look to Pema?
qa.a: Pema saw a student who sounded very sure and very tired, and chose to get help calmly rather than argue about chance.

passage:
Dec 27, hostel, most people gone home
Lost again tonight. Started with the 500 I won last week, telling myself I'd play only that. Lost it by ten. Then I thought: five losses in a row, the cards HAVE to turn now, a win is due. Put in another 1,000. Lost. Another. Lost.
Jaya came in at 1 am for water and saw my face. I told her it's fine, one good hand and I'm back to zero.
She said, "Indu, you said that on Christmas too."
I didn't answer. I keep doing the maths in my head: the longer I lose, the closer the big win must be. It feels so logical while I'm playing.
Jaya left a sticky note on my laptop with the student counselling number. It's still there. I haven't moved it.

qa.a: A sticky note with the student counselling number.

qa.a: After a losing streak a win feels due and logical, so Indu feels hopeful and driven to win it back, even as the losses grow.

qa.q: What would you advise Indu to do next?
